title: Scaling writes: hierarchical aggregation
seriesDescription: How to scale write-heavy systems in an interview: vertical scaling and database choice, sharding and partition keys, vertical partitioning, queues and load shedding, batching, hierarchical aggregation, and the resharding and hot-key deep dives.
description: Reducing volume in stages for high-volume counters and live feeds, using the live comments example.
source: Study notes: the scaling writes pattern

questions.prompt: What is the core idea of hierarchical aggregation?

options.text: Process data in stages, reducing the volume at each step by combining events.
options.why: Right: build aggregated views incrementally.

options.text: Store every event individually forever.
options.why: It avoids that for extreme volume.

options.text: Send every write straight to the root without any extra configuration.
options.why: That recreates the bottleneck.

options.text: Delete all data older than a second in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Unrelated; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: It suits analytics and stream processing where aggregated views are enough.

questions.prompt: In live comments with millions of viewers, why write to broadcast nodes rather than directly to every viewer?

options.text: Writing to M broadcast nodes instead of N viewers reduces the number of writes any system handles.
options.why: Right: broadcast nodes forward to their viewers.

options.text: Viewers cannot receive messages directly without any extra configuration in a typical production setup.
options.why: The point is volume, not capability.

options.text: It makes all viewers see different data for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
options.why: They want the same eventually consistent view.

options.text: It removes the need for any servers.
options.why: Servers are still needed.

questions.explanation: Assign viewers to broadcast nodes with consistent hashing.

questions.prompt: What problem remains after adding broadcast nodes, and how is it solved?

options.text: The root receives events from all viewers; write processors aggregate over a window and forward batches.
options.why: Right: aggregate on the way in, disaggregate on the way out.

options.text: The viewers need bigger screens, so use larger fonts as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Not a technical solution.

options.text: The broadcast nodes need to be removed without any extra configuration in a typical production setup.
options.why: They are part of the solution.

options.text: Comments must be dropped entirely.
options.why: Aggregation avoids that.

questions.explanation: Write processors are chosen by comment id, so each owns the counts for its comments.

questions.prompt: How are write processors chosen for likes on comments?

options.text: By the id of the comment being liked, so one processor owns each comment's count.
options.why: Right: all likes for a comment meet in one place.

options.text: By the id of the viewer, so likes are scattered for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
options.why: Counts would be split across processors.

options.text: At random for each like as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: The root would have to merge huge duplicates.

options.text: By the time of day.
options.why: That would not group likes by comment.

questions.explanation: The root then only merges small batches of totals.

questions.prompt: True or false: hierarchical aggregation reduces the writes any one component handles at the cost of added latency from the extra steps.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: that is the trade-off.

options.text: False
options.why: It does add latency; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: Each stage waits for a window, so results are slightly delayed.

questions.prompt: Which workload benefits most from batching and hierarchical aggregation?

options.text: High-volume analytics or numeric data like counts, views and likes.
options.why: Right: often 5-10x improvements.

options.text: Low-volume configuration changes for most everyday workloads.
options.why: No pressure there; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Large binary uploads like videos.
options.why: They are not aggregated.

options.text: A single record updated once a day without any extra configuration in a typical production setup.
options.why: Nothing to combine; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: Look for data that can be summed or merged.
